# The First Shadow

In the beginning, when the world was newly formed, there lived a young weaver named Lyra who created tapestries of such beauty that even the sun would pause to admire them. She worked tirelessly from dawn until dusk, her fingers dancing across the loom.

One day, the sun grew jealous. "Why do you only work when I shine?" it asked. "Do you not trust the darkness?"

"I cannot see in darkness," Lyra replied simply.

The sun, moved by her honesty, made a bargain. "I will give you a gift—a piece of myself that follows you always, so you may never forget the light."

That evening, as the sun set, Lyra noticed something strange trailing behind her—a dark silhouette that mimicked her every move. She tried to run from it, but it followed faithfully.

Finally, she understood. The shadow was not darkness, but proof that light had touched her. It was the sun's promise that even in the deepest night, she would remember the day.

From then on, every living thing received a shadow, a reminder that light and darkness are eternal partners, neither complete without the other.

And Lyra's tapestries grew even more beautiful, for she learned to weave with both.

# The Tale of the First Echo

Long ago, when the world was newly formed, a young spirit named Lyra possessed the most beautiful voice in all creation. She would sing to the mountains, the rivers, and the sky, filling the silence with melodies that made flowers bloom and stars shine brighter.

One day, Lyra fell deeply in love with her own voice. She sang only for herself, climbing to the highest peak where no one else could hear. She refused to share her gift with the world below, believing her songs were too precious for others.

The mountain, moved by her selfishness, decided to teach her a lesson. As Lyra sang her favorite melody, the mountain caught her voice and sent it back to her—but changed, hollow, lonely. Lyra heard herself and wept, finally understanding how empty beauty becomes when hoarded.

She tried to apologize, but the mountain only returned her words, again and again.

The gods took pity on Lyra and transformed her into wind, forever traveling the world, carrying songs to every canyon and cave. And so echoes were born—a reminder that the most beautiful things are meant to be shared, and that selfishness only returns emptiness.

To this day, when you shout into a canyon, you hear Lyra's lesson returning to you.

"I cannot carry all of this alone," she cried out to the heavens.

The mountain heard her plea and offered a solution. "Give your memories to me," it said, "and I will hold them in my stones and caves."

Kael drew water only from the bright river, believing darkness would taint his clay. His pots were beautiful but brittle, shattering at the slightest touch.

One twilight, the River of Shadows spoke: "Why do you fear me? Your work is incomplete."

"I seek only purity," Kael replied.

"Then you seek only half of truth," the river whispered. "Light without shadow has no depth. Strength comes from balance."

Reluctantly, Kael mixed waters from both rivers. The clay felt different—heavier, richer. He shaped a simple bowl and set it to dry.

When he returned, he found it transformed. The vessel bore patterns he hadn't carved—swirls of light and dark dancing together, each defining the other. And it was unbreakable.

Kael understood then that wholeness requires both illumination and mystery, joy and sorrow, giving and receiving. He taught others to honor both rivers, and their pottery became legendary.

Thus we learned: true beauty emerges not from choosing light over darkness, but from weaving them together into something stronger than either alone.
